title: Travelling and Getting About
summary: The verb that carries the manner of the going and the prefix that carries its direction; the station against the stop; buying a ticket; the different forms left and right take for going and for standing; asking the way; and the language of a timetable.

sources.citation: Ambrazas, Vytautas (ed.), *Lithuanian Grammar*. Vilnius: Baltos lankos, 1997.
sources.note: Descriptive source for the paradigms and rule statements on this page.

sources.citation: *Dabartinės lietuvių kalbos žodynas*, Lietuvių kalbos institutas.
sources.note: Citation forms, government and register for this section's vocabulary.

rules.heading: Going, and the Manner of Going
rules.statement: Lithuanian names the manner of the going in the verb itself: **eiti** on foot, **važiuoti** by land vehicle, **skristi** by air, **plaukti** by water (¶64). **Keliauti** is to travel as an occupation of the day rather than a single journey, and **vykti** is the word of a timetable and an official notice.

examples.target: Į darbą einu pėsčiomis, o namo važiuoju autobusu.
examples.gloss: I walk to work and go home by bus.
Tomorrow we fly to London.
In the summer we travel around Lithuania.

paradigms.caption: The manner in the verb

rows.label: vykti
cells: proceeding — of a timetable or a notice

paradigms.footnote: The vehicle itself stands in the instrumental (¶73): *važiuoju autobusu*, *skrendu lėktuvu*.

rules.heading: The Prefixes of Coming and Going
rules.statement: A prefix fixes the direction of the going, and the same set serves every verb of motion: **at-** here, **iš-** away, **nu-** off there, **par-** back home, **į-** in, **pri-** up to. *Ateiti* and *atvykti*, *išeiti* and *išvykti*, differ only in the manner the root carries.

examples.gloss: The train arrives at two o'clock.
He left an hour ago.
The children came home from school.

paradigms.caption: One root, six directions

rows.label: nueiti
cells: to go off, to get somewhere

paradigms.footnote: **Grįžti** returns to any place at all; **pareiti** and **parvažiuoti** return home in particular.

footnotes: A reflexive verb keeps its affix behind the prefix: *sukti* → *pasisukti* (¶179).

rules.heading: Stotis and Stotelė
rules.statement: **Stotis** is a station — a building with a timetable, a ticket office and platforms. **Stotelė**, its diminutive, is a stop: a post at the roadside where a bus halts. Air travel has neither, but **oro uostas**, the air harbour.

examples.gloss: The railway station is in the town centre.
Get off at the third stop.
A bus runs from the airport.

footnotes: *Stotis* is a third-declension feminine in *-is*: *stoties, stočiai, stotį* (¶170).
**Autobusų stotis** is the coach station, and **autobuso stotelė** the bus stop; the genitive plural and singular are as much of the difference as the suffix is.

rules.heading: The Ticket
rules.statement: A ticket is bought **į** a place with the accusative, and its kinds are named by an adjective: **vienkartinis** for one journey, **mėnesinis** for a month. The return journey is **pirmyn ir atgal**, and a one-way ticket is **į vieną pusę**.

examples.gloss: Two tickets to Kaunas, please.
The ticket must be bought before boarding.
One return ticket.

footnotes: **Vienkartinis** and **mėnesinis** are of the *-inis* type, whose feminine is *-inė* (¶164).

rules.heading: Left and Right, Going and Standing
rules.statement: Direction and position take different forms of the same word: **į kairę** and **į dešinę** are *to the left* and *to the right*, while **kairėje** and **dešinėje** are *on the left* and *on the right*. The turning itself is **sukti** or **pasukti**, and *tiesiai* is straight on.

examples.target: Eikite tiesiai, paskui sukite į kairę.
examples.gloss: Go straight on, then turn left.
The pharmacy is on the right, by the crossroads.
Round the corner you will find the stop.

paradigms.caption: Going and standing
paradigms.footnote: The accusative after *į* is the case of motion towards, and the locative the case of rest (¶61, ¶59).

rules.heading: Asking the Way
rules.statement: The way is asked with **Kaip nueiti iki …?** on foot and **Kaip nuvažiuoti iki …?** by vehicle, the infinitive standing after the question word and *iki* taking the genitive (¶33). *Ar toli?* asks the distance and *Kiek reikia eiti?* the time.

examples.gloss: Excuse me, how do I get to the station?
How do I get to the airport?

examples.target: Ar toli iki centro? — Ne, dešimt minučių pėsčiomis.
examples.gloss: Is it far to the centre? — No, ten minutes on foot.

footnotes: *Iki* marks the point reached and *į* the place entered: *iki stoties* stops at the door, *į stotį* goes inside.

rules.heading: The Timetable, and Being Late
rules.statement: A timetable says when a service **išvyksta** and when it **atvyksta**, and the hour stands in the accusative (¶83). **Vėluoti** is to be running late and **pavėluoti į** with the accusative is to have missed something; **spėti** is to be in time for it.

examples.target: Traukinys išvyksta septintą, o atvyksta devintą.
examples.gloss: The train leaves at seven and arrives at nine.
The bus is ten minutes late.

examples.target: Nespėjau į traukinį, teko laukti valandą.
examples.gloss: I missed the train and had to wait an hour.

footnotes: **Persėsti** is to change from one service to another: *persėdau Kaune*.

vocabulary.gloss: to go, to proceed (of a service or an official journey)
to go off, to get to (on foot)
to be late for (+ į and acc.)

vocabulary.notes: Third declension; the stop at the roadside is stotelė.
Pirmyn ir atgal is a return journey.

drills.stem: Complete: **Rytoj ____ į Londoną.** (Tomorrow we fly to London.)
drills.explanation: The manner of the going is in the verb, and **skristi** is by air (¶225). *Važiuoti* is by land vehicle, *eiti* on foot, *plaukti* by water.

drills.stem: Where does a bus halt at the roadside?
drills.explanation: **Stotelė** is the stop and **stotis** the station — a building with a timetable and a ticket office (¶227). The diminutive suffix is the whole of the difference in form.

drills.stem: Which word fits: **Eikite tiesiai, paskui sukite ____.** (turn left)
drills.explanation: Turning is motion, and motion takes **į** with the accusative (¶61, ¶229). *Kairėje* is the locative and says where something already stands.

drills.stem: Which verb fits: **Vaikai jau ____ iš mokyklos.** (The children have come home from school.)
drills.explanation: **Par-** is the prefix of coming home (¶226). *Atėjo* is arriving anywhere, *išėjo* is leaving, *nuėjo* is going off somewhere else.
The way is asked with an infinitive after the question word, and *nueiti* is the one that goes on foot (¶230, ¶225). *Iki* takes the genitive — *iki stoties* (¶33).
A ticket is bought **į** a place, with the accusative (¶228, ¶61). *Iki* marks the point reached and belongs to asking the way; *pas* is used of people only (¶139).
**Iš-** is the prefix of going away, so *išvykti* is to depart and *atvykti* to arrive (¶226, ¶231). The hour stands in the accusative (¶83).

drills.stem: Which of these are said of a vehicle rather than of a person on foot?
drills.explanation: *Važiuoti* is by land vehicle, so both its prefixed forms are (¶225, ¶226). *Pareiti* is on foot, and *skristi* is by air, which is neither.

drills.stem: Match each prefixed verb with what the prefix says about the going.
drills.explanation: *At-* marks arrival whatever the root, so *atvykti* and *ateiti* take the same label and differ only in the manner of the going (¶226). *Iš-* is away and *par-* is home. Nothing here goes in, which would be *į-*.

options: Į darbą einu pėsčiomis, o namo važiuoju autobusu.
Į darbą einu pėsčiomis, o namo einu autobusu.
Į darbą važiuoju pėsčiomis, o namo važiuoju autobusu.
Į darbą einu pėsčiomis, o namo važiuoju autobusą.
drills.explanation: The verb has to agree with the manner: *eiti* on foot and *važiuoti* by vehicle (¶225). The vehicle stands in the instrumental (¶73), so *autobusą* in the fourth is a case too far.

drills.stem: In **Nespėjau į traukinį, todėl teko laukti valandą**, which statements are true?
options: *Nespėti į* is to have missed something.
drills.explanation: *Todėl* gives the consequence and *nes* the cause (¶107): the missing came first and the waiting followed. *Spėti į* and *pavėluoti į* both take the accusative (¶231), and duration is accusative too (¶83).

drills.stem: **Vaistinė yra ____, o dabar sukite ____.** Which pair completes it? (on the right … to the right)
drills.explanation: Rest takes the locative and motion the accusative after *į* (¶59, ¶61, ¶229). The two halves of the sentence want different forms of the same word, which is what the second option gets exactly backwards.

options: Autobusų stotis yra centre, o autobuso stotelė — už kampo.
Autobusų stotelė yra centre, o autobuso stotis — už kampo.
Autobusų stotis yra centre, o autobuso stotis — už kampo.
Autobusų stotelė yra centre, o autobuso stotelė — už kampo.
drills.explanation: The coach station is a building and the stop is a post at the roadside (¶227); *už kampo* fits the second and not the first. The genitive in front of each names what it serves — *autobusų* plural for the station, *autobuso* singular for the stop.

drills.stem: A timetable reads: **Išvyksta aštuntą valandą, atvyksta vienuoliktą valandą.** Kiek valandų trunka kelionė?
drills.explanation: From the eighth hour to the eleventh. Both hours stand in the accusative, as the hour of an action does (¶83, ¶231).

drills.stem: Lithuanian names its cases in a fixed order: *vardininkas, kilmininkas, naudininkas, galininkas, įnagininkas, vietininkas, šauksmininkas*. Counting from the first, what position does the case of *stoties* hold in **Kaip nueiti iki stoties?**
drills.explanation: *Stoties* is the *kilmininkas*, the genitive, which *iki* governs (¶33, ¶230). *Stotis* is a third-declension noun, so its genitive is *stoties* and not *stotės* (¶170).
drills.unit: position in the order of cases

drills.title: Kaip nuvažiuoti į oro uostą
drills.passage:
TURISTAS. Atsiprašau, ar galite padėti? Kaip nuvažiuoti iki oro uosto?
PRAEIVIS. Galite važiuoti autobusu arba traukiniu. Traukinys greitesnis.
TURISTAS. O kur yra stotis?
PRAEIVIS. Eikite tiesiai iki sankryžos, paskui sukite į kairę. Stotis bus dešinėje, už didelio pastato.
TURISTAS. Ar toli?
PRAEIVIS. Ne, dešimt minučių pėsčiomis. Bet skubėkite: traukinys išvyksta ketvirtą valandą, o kitas tik po dviejų valandų.
TURISTAS. Ačiū! O kur pirkti bilietą?
PRAEIVIS. Stotyje, prie kasos. Bilietas į vieną pusę kainuoja du eurus.
TURISTAS. Ar reikia persėsti?
PRAEIVIS. Ne, traukinys važiuoja tiesiai į oro uostą. Geros kelionės!
drills.translation:
TOURIST. Excuse me, can you help? How do I get to the airport?
PASSER-BY. You can go by bus or by train. The train is quicker.
TOURIST. And where is the station?
PASSER-BY. Go straight on to the crossroads, then turn left. The station will be on the right, behind a large building.
TOURIST. Is it far?
PASSER-BY. No, ten minutes on foot. But hurry: the train leaves at four o'clock, and the next one only in two hours.
TOURIST. Thank you! And where do I buy a ticket?
PASSER-BY. At the station, at the ticket window. A one-way ticket costs two euros.
TOURIST. Do I have to change?
PASSER-BY. No, the train goes straight to the airport. Have a good journey!

options: Tiesiai iki sankryžos, paskui į kairę.
Tiesiai iki sankryžos, paskui į dešinę.
questions.explanation: *Eikite tiesiai iki sankryžos, paskui sukite į kairę.* The station then stands *dešinėje* — on the right — which is a position and not a second turning (¶229).
*Stotyje, prie kasos.* The locative places the buying inside the building, and *prie* with the genitive puts it at the ticket window (¶59, ¶33).
*Ne, traukinys važiuoja tiesiai į oro uostą.* *Persėsti* is to change from one service to another (¶231).

questions.stem: Which statements about the passer-by's directions are true?
options: *Į kairę* is an accusative of motion.
*Už didelio pastato* is an accusative after *už*.
questions.explanation: *Už* of place takes the genitive — *už didelio pastato* — and only *už* of payment and thanks takes the accusative (¶141, ¶33). The rest is the direction-and-position pair of ¶229.

questions.stem: Kiek eurų kainuoja bilietas į vieną pusę?
questions.explanation: *Bilietas į vieną pusę kainuoja du eurus.* The numeral takes the accusative plural as the object of *kainuoti* (¶54, ¶58, ¶228).

questions.stem: The passer-by says **Geros kelionės!** Why the genitive?
options: Because a wish stands in the genitive, as *viso gero* and *skanaus* do.
questions.explanation: A wish is made in the genitive and needs no verb (¶148, ¶159): *viso gero*, *skanaus*, *sveikatos*, *geros kelionės*. There is no preposition in the phrase at all.

sources.note: A street dialogue, kept to the motion verbs, prefixes and directions of ¶225–¶231.
